analysis.one_liner: Shields businesses, health care providers, and employers from COVID-related lawsuits and federal workplace-safety penalties.
analysis.headline: Referred to two House committees in July 2020 with 7 cosponsors, and never received a vote before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have barred most lawsuits over the spread of COVID-19, protecting businesses, schools, universities, nonprofits, and health care providers from civil claims unless the injured person could prove willful misconduct, gross negligence, or similar extreme behavior. It would also have barred federal workplace-safety citations and penalties against employers whose only COVID-related violation was failing to follow safety rules, so long as the employer made 'reasonable efforts' to comply with guidance. The protections would have covered cases dating back to January 1, 2020, and lasted until 18 months after the end of the COVID-19 public health emergency, and they would have overridden stricter state laws.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses, employers, schools, universities, nonprofits, and health care providers facing potential lawsuits or federal penalties over COVID-19 exposure. The shield would cover conduct back to January 1, 2020, including claims already filed, so companies facing pending suits would benefit immediately.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Employers and health care providers facing COVID lawsuits

how_it_helps.text: Bars civil liability for the spread or possible transmission of SARS-CoV-2 for any person acting in good faith — defined broadly to include corporations, partnerships, universities, schools, nonprofits, and religious organizations — from January 1, 2020 to 18 months after the end of the emergency period.
Carries the shield into federal and state court by preempting state laws that are inconsistent with it, while allowing states to keep only laws that provide greater liability protection.
Exempts health care providers acting in good faith from liability for COVID transmission during pandemic-impacted care, including care delivered by someone working under a professional's supervision.

Amends the Occupational Safety and Health Act so the government cannot issue citations, and employers face no civil or criminal penalties, for COVID-related workplace safety violations if the employer 'acted in good faith' by making reasonable efforts to follow guidance.
Applies retroactively to cases filed before, on, or after enactment, and limits damages from COVID infection to cases involving death, 48-hour hospitalization, or permanent impairment.

analysis.who_pays: Workers, patients, and their families who contracted COVID-19 in a workplace, nursing home, or care setting. Their ability to recover for illness or death would depend on meeting a 'clear and convincing evidence' standard for gross negligence or worse — one of the highest proof standards in law — and infection that did not cause 'serious bodily injury' would not support damages at all.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers and patients exposed to COVID-19

drawbacks.text: Injured workers and their families would lose ordinary legal remedies: the bill requires clear and convincing evidence of willful, reckless, or grossly negligent conduct before any recovery, and excludes damages for COVID infection that is not 'serious bodily injury.'

The OSHA exemption would leave the federal government with no citation or penalty tool for COVID-related workplace safety violations, at a time when many essential workers had no option to stay home, and 'good faith' is defined by an employer's own 'reasonable efforts' to follow guidance rather than by actual compliance.

Supporters argued a broad shield was needed because litigation fears were discouraging businesses from reopening and providers from serving patients during the emergency; opponents countered that without legal exposure, employers had less incentive to follow safety rules. The bill's narrow carve-outs (gross negligence and above) and its sunset 18 months after the emergency are the concessions its authors made to that objection, but critics said they were not enough.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits flow almost entirely to employers and providers in the form of removed legal exposure, while the costs fall on sick workers and patients who would have to clear a very high legal bar to recover anything. The gross-negligence carve-out and sunset show some attempt at balance, but because 'good faith' is judged by reasonable efforts rather than results, an employer that made token efforts while spreading infection would still be shielded. On balance the bill trades away ordinary people's legal protections for business certainty.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Judiciary and Education and Labor committees in July 2020, neither committee acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Garret Graves (R-LA) introduced the bill on July 9, 2020, during the pandemic reopening debate, with five original cosponsors.
The Speaker referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary and, in addition, to the Committee on Education and Labor.
It drew 7 cosponsors — 5 of 197 House Republicans and 2 of 231 House Democrats.
No committee reported the bill, no floor vote was ever scheduled, and the action history shows no activity after the day of referral.
The CRS summary describes it as limiting civil liability for COVID transmission and exempting employers from certain occupational safety and health penalties.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers, patients, and their families kept their right to sue employers and businesses over COVID exposure; employers did not get the federal liability shield or the OSHA penalty exemption they sought. Health care providers also remained exposed to COVID-related suits, though no such federal shield exists to this day.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Workers and patients, who kept their legal remedies

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and 5 of the 7 cosponsors were Republicans; the two Democratic cosponsors were conservative members from Texas and Minnesota. No roll-call votes were ever taken.

industries.industry: Employers (retail, hospitality, manufacturing, nursing homes, and other businesses open during the pandemic)
industries.note: The bill would have wiped out most COVID-related lawsuits against them — including suits already filed — and eliminated federal OSHA citations and penalties for COVID safety violations when an employer made 'reasonable efforts' to follow guidance. The gain comes directly at the cost of workers and families who got sick at work and would otherwise be able to recover.

Providers and their supervising staff would be shielded from COVID-transmission suits during pandemic care, reducing malpractice-style risk at a moment of crisis. The cost is to patients harmed by substandard care, who would need clear and convincing evidence of gross negligence or worse to recover anything.

A five-year window (from January 2020 until 18 months after the emergency ended) of sharply reduced pandemic claims would cut insurers' exposure on business and medical liability policies. Ordinary people's uncompensated losses are the mirror image of that saving.
